newsitem.title: USA: U.S. energy head applauds distillate stock rebound.
newsitem.headline: U.S. energy head applauds distillate stock rebound.

text.p: U.S. Energy Secretary Hazel O'Leary said she is pleased with the results of her consultations with the oil industry on actions to avert a shortage of heating oil stocks this winter.
O'Leary, speaking to reporters after giving a talk to the Foreign Policy Association in New York, cautioned, however, that she was taking a "wait and see approach" before calling the issue settled.
"We have to watch and we have to stay on it. I like the response we got from industry," O'Leary said.

O'Leary met with a number of oil executives two weeks ago in an effort to combat historically low levels of distillate stocks, which have driven heating oil prices sharply higher. A number of U.S. congressmen -- mainly from northeastern states where heating oil consumers predominate -- have called for government intervention to stem the price rises of 20 to 25 cents per gallon.
O'Leary rejected the calls for intervention, saying it was not the role of her department "to go shaking our fingers under people's noses."

Since her meeting with industry executives, O'Leary said "we've seen production of distillates go out of the roof. Producers have been standing on their heads in the last four to five weeks to keep up with demand."

The latest American Petroleum Insititute (API) inventory report released on Tuesday, showed distillate stocks building, or increasing by some 3.6 million barrels. Most importantly, heating oil stocks in the East Coast region grew by 2.8 million barrels for the week ended October 25.
Even with the recent growth in stock levels, the East Coast region's inventories are 34 percent shy of last year's levels, 14.7 million barrels down.
O'Leary said stocks remain vulnerable to sustained cold weather spells, leaving her guarded to possible inventory declines, but she emphasised that immediate signs were favourable.
"You see with the prices dropping both here and in Europe, that (distillate supply) is likely to stay in the United States...that is a good sign."
O'Leary said the short-term efforts by industry to open more pipeline space and curtail planned maintenance for some crude units around the country has boosted stocks.
Later this year, O'Leary said start-ups for new North Sea production will ease supply concerns further, as will new field development in Venezuela's Orinoco region.
